notes.meaning: The writer remembers a time of deep trouble when he cried out to the Lord, and God answered him. This begins a collection of songs sung by pilgrims as they traveled up to Jerusalem for the yearly festivals. Remembering how God has answered our prayers in the past gives us courage to pray again today.

The psalmist begs God to rescue his life from people who spread malicious lies and false accusations against him. Slander has brought him into great danger, and human effort alone cannot stop the harm being done. Only the Lord has the power to silence deceitful tongues and protect the innocent.

The speaker addresses the lying tongue directly, asking what kind of punishment awaits it from God. Those who use words to wound others often think they will escape, but the Lord holds every deceiver accountable. Their craftiness will ultimately turn to their own ruin.

God will judge the deceitful tongue like a warrior shooting sharp arrows. His punishment is also compared to burning coals of the broom tree, a desert wood that burns with fierce heat and stays hot for a very long time. God's righteous judgment fits the fiery, destructive damage that slander causes to others.

The writer grieves that he feels like an exile living in Meshech and Kedar. Meshech was a distant land far to the north, and Kedar was a desert tribe in Arabia, both known as harsh and warlike peoples. He uses these names as symbols for the cruel, quarrelsome neighbors who surround him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Following the older Greek and Latin texts, the traditional Douay-Rheims translation reads the word Meshech as meaning a prolonged stay, understanding the verse as sorrow over an exile that has dragged on too long.

notes.meaning: The psalmist laments that he has spent far too much time among people who despise living in harmony. His companions hate the very idea of peace and thrive on constant hostility. Living alongside people who reject God's peace is an exhausting burden for the faithful.

The writer longs for peace and speaks kindly to resolve conflict, but his neighbors only want war. Whenever he makes an effort to live at peace, they use it as an opportunity to attack. Even when others respond to kindness with hostility, God's people must continue to pursue peace.
